extracted.intended_audience: attorneys/practitioners who represent clients before the USPTO in trademark matters (including U.S. counsel for foreign-domiciled trademark applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and professional-conduct standards the USPTO uses to evaluate and discipline practitioners in trademark matters, including signature rules, certification duties, competency/diligence obligations, TEAS electronic-signature procedures, and required controls when working with foreign referring entities or suspended practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule (37 C.F.R. § 2.11(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective August 3, 2019, any foreign-domiciled trademark applicant or registrant must be represented before the USPTO by an attorney who is licensed to practice law in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule was intended to (1) increase compliance with U.S. trademark law and USPTO regulations, (2) improve the accuracy of trademark submissions to the USPTO, and (3) safeguard the integrity of the U.S. trademark register. Practitioners serving as U.S. counsel for foreign-domiciled clients are expected to know and follow this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO trademark signature rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 2.193(a),(c),(e); 11.18(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures on trademark documents must be signed by a proper person; trademark documents must be personally signed by the signatory named on the document; an electronic signature must be personally entered and placed between two forward slash ("/") symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the signature fails to comply because it was entered by someone other than the named signatory or not signed by a proper person, the trademark may be subject to cancellation or invalidation. The USPTO relies on signed declarations; false statements may implicate criminal penalties (18 U.S.C. § 1001).

rubrics_metrics.name: TMEP guidance on electronic signatures (TMEP § 611.01(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: All documents must be personally signed; the person identified as the signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature; another person (e.g., paralegal, assistant, or secretary) may not sign or type the electronic signature of a practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Just as signing the name of another person on paper does not serve as the signature of the person whose name is written, typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature by that person." The TMEP gives clear, straightforward guidance that electronic signatures must be personally entered by the named signatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of improper or inauthentic signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Signatures entered by an improper person or not personally entered by the named signatory can render filings invalid and jeopardize the integrity of the federal trademark registration process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improperly signed filings may lead to cancellation/invalidity of registrations and disciplinary action against practitioners; the Order cites multiple precedent disciplinary decisions and T.T.A.B./BPAI cases supporting adverse consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: TEAS signature method — DIRECT
rubrics_metrics.description: "DIRECT" is TEAS' default signature procedure: the named signatory signs directly at the end of the document by personally entering their chosen characters between forward slashes at time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a document is saved for later filing, electronic signature is not saved and must be reentered personally by the signatory at filing (presumption document may be modified). This reentry requirement ensures the signer personally verifies the facts at the time of filing (see In re Shia).

rubrics_metrics.name: TEAS signature method — E-SIGN ON
rubrics_metrics.description: "E-SIGN ON" involves TEAS sending a hyperlink via email to the designated signatory who opens the link, electronically signs, and the signed form is returned to the preparer; the preparer then finalizes submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To use E-SIGN-ON the preparer selects "E-mail Text Form to second party for signature," enters signatory details and clicks "Validate," sends the text form, and the signatory completes signing via the emailed link. The form must be signed and the filing completed within 14 days (the 14-day period starts when the requestor clicks the send link); undeliverable notices alert the preparer to email problems. The protocol creates an audit trail of communications between requestor and signatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: TEAS signature method — H SIGN (handwritten signature image)
rubrics_metrics.description: "H SIGN" allows submission of an electronic file (e.g., JPG) of an original handwritten pen-and-ink signature attached to the TEAS filing; preparer typically prints, has signatory sign by hand, scans/attaches image, then files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under H SIGN the original application is saved using the Download Portable form button on the Validation Page. Practitioners must ensure the attached handwritten signature image is genuine and that the filed text form matches the reviewed materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner certifications when presenting papers (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner certifies that statements on papers are true on the practitioner's knowledge, and that statements made on information and belief are believed to be true; the practitioner also certifies they have conducted an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific certification elements include: (i) paper is not presented for improper purpose (harass/delay/increase costs); (ii) legal contentions are warranted by law or nonfrivolous argument; (iii) factual contentions have evidentiary support or likely will after investigation; (iv) denials of factual contentions are warranted or reasonably based on lack of information. Violations may jeopardize probative value and lead to criminal penalties (18 U.S.C. § 1001) and discipline (§ 11.18(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to conduct an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances (support for factual assertions and specimens)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before presenting factual assertions (including specimens) to the USPTO, the practitioner must have conducted a reasonable inquiry under the circumstances to support those assertions as required by § 11.18.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to conduct a reasonable inquiry can result in Office Actions, disciplinary consequences, and potential criminal liability; the Final Order cites specimen-review failures (in sample: 61.5% of Office Actions related to specimens; 21.5% due to suspected digital/altered images) as examples of inadequate inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall provide competent representation to clients, which includes knowing and understanding relevant USPTO rules (e.g., signature rules), maintaining adequate means to receive USPTO/client correspondence, and having controls to ensure filings comply with USPTO requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of incompetence include not having access to or means to receive correspondence for thousands of transferred matters, lacking controls to verify filings prepared/mailed by third parties, and failing to supervise use of an attorney's signature or credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable diligence and promptness in representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing clients; failures include not having adequate means of receiving correspondence, not having controls to monitor third-party actions, and failing to adequately review specimens or otherwise conduct a reasonable inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the Order: not monitoring 3,900 transferred matters' correspondence, relying on suspended practitioner's email, failing to verify that filed applications matched reviewed materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor toward the USPTO (37 C.F.R. § 11.303 and related provisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must be candid toward the USPTO and must not knowingly authorize or instruct non-practitioners to sign the practitioner's name on trademark documents, including declarations, filed with the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowingly authorizing non-practitioners to sign undermines candor and integrity; multiple cited decisions discipline practitioners who allowed others to sign their names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities regarding non-practitioner assistance (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not authorize non-practitioners to sign the practitioner's name to trademark documents filed with the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting, authorizing, or instructing non-practitioners to sign is a violation; practitioners must supervise and control non-practitioner assistance to prevent improper signatures or filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assisting unauthorized practice before the USPTO (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must not assist another person in engaging in the unlawful practice of trademark law before the USPTO (e.g., enabling non-practitioners or suspended practitioners to prepare/submit filings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assistance that enables unauthorized practice (including aiding non-practitioners or suspended practitioners to act) can result in discipline and may be treated as conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must not engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice, such as authorizing non-practitioners to sign, failing to have adequate controls over filings, or allowing a suspended practitioner to continue practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order cites lack of controls and specimen-review failures as examples of conduct that prejudices administration of justice; such conduct formed part of the basis for discipline in the cited proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct that adversely reflects on fitness to practice before the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must avoid other conduct that would adversely reflect on their fitness to practice before the USPTO; failures to ensure compliance with USPTO rules and inadequate supervisory controls can qualify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts and omissions as U.S. counsel that do not reasonably ensure compliance with trademark rules/regulations may be grounds for discipline under this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate controls over client correspondence and representation after transfers (Change of Address/Representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When matters are transferred (e.g., via CAR forms), the attorney of record must ensure they have access to and means to receive USPTO and third-party correspondence (i.e., not leave another practitioner's email as the correspondence address), and must implement reasonable controls to monitor incoming communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to change correspondence email or to monitor another practitioner's email (especially a suspended practitioner's) is a deficiency evidencing lack of competence and diligence; the Order found Respondent lacked adequate controls for ~3,900 transferred matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls and verification when using foreign referring entities or third-party portals (e.g., Baiyue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who work with foreign referring entities or who rely on third-party software/media must have reasonably adequate controls to verify that (a) the materials they reviewed are identical to the materials filed, (b) their signature images are not used without consent, and (c) filings submitted by the third party were actually filed with the practitioner's knowledge and consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order warns that relying on a proprietary portal and uploading a signature image without verifying the final TEAS filing can lead to unauthorized or altered filings. Practitioners must ensure authentication, auditing, and verification processes when outsourcing or collaborating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate review of specimens and factual support for specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must competently review specimens submitted to the USPTO and conduct a reasonable inquiry into whether specimens are genuine and supported by evidence before presenting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical example: in a sample of 500 applications, 61.5% of Office Actions were for specimen issues and 21.5% were because specimens appeared digitally created/altered — illustrating the need for careful specimen review and investigation per § 11.18.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligations when dealing with matters of a suspended practitioner (37 C.F.R. § 11.58)
rubrics_metrics.description: If involved with a practitioner who is suspended, practitioners must ensure compliance with suspension restrictions (e.g., suspended practitioner prohibited from practicing, communicating with others about matters, or meeting with USPTO on those matters), and must not enable the suspended practitioner to continue unauthorized activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent was required to comply with § 11.58; accepting matters from a suspended practitioner without proper controls (e.g., retaining suspended practitioner's email as correspondence address) is improper and can be the basis for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner expected to know and consult USPTO resources (TMEP, rules, OED decisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are reasonably expected to know the laws, rules, regulations, procedures, and available USPTO resources (e.g., TMEP, USPTO trademark web pages, OED decisions) relevant to their representation before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order emphasizes readily available materials (tmep.uspto.gov, www.uspto.gov/trademarks, OED FOIA reading room) and lists many precedent disciplinary decisions to show information is accessible and that ignorance is not an excuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial/disciplinary measures and compliance obligations upon discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: When discipline is imposed, the practitioner may be suspended, placed on probation, given limited recognition to finish matters, required to provide client notice, required to search and report on matters identifying them as attorney of record, to dissociate from accounts/customer numbers, and to cooperate with investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order specifies sanctions imposed (five-month suspension, 30-day limited recognition, 12-month probation with bi-weekly database searches and 90-day reporting, potential additional suspension for probation violations, disabling/suspending USPTO accounts, dissociation from customer numbers, obligation to email translated Final Order to foreign clients under conditions, and cooperation with inquiries into third-party improper filings). These are examples of the types of remedial steps the Office may require.
